name: Ufnun
bio: Suraim ibn Ma'shar, called Ufnun, of the Hubaib branch of Taghlib, lived before the promulgation of Islam, probably while his tribe was settled in 'Iraq. Lyall thinks he may have been a Christian.
Lyall gives the story that a diviner had warned him he would die at a place called Ilahah, where a snake bit him on a journey to Damascus.

poems.title: Ode LXV: Alas! nought can I avail
poems.author: Ufnun
poems.note: Lyall's heading: Suraim son of Ma'shar, of Hubaib, of Taghlib, called Ufnun.
poems.text:
Alas! nought can I avail — Mu'awiyah, go thy way!- nor yet the fond women who follow the rede of the soothsayers.

No profit is there to a man who strives to deceive his soul, who wails over Fate and cries: 'Ah, would that my lot were thus!'

So tread forward : many the ways by which a man's death may come, and all thou canst give will not redeem thee a single life.

Yea, no man there is who knows a shield for his soul from Doom, unless it be God himself that stands as his Lord and Shield.

Ah, sorrow enough, that my kin will journey to-morrow on, and I shall be left for aye to lie in Ilahah's ground!

poems.title: Ode LXVI: Carry my message to Hubaib, and
poems.author: Ufnun
poems.text:
Carry my message to Hubaib, and drive into the minds of their chiefs, that my heart is estranged from them and full of sadness.

I used, aforetime, to outstrip easily those who raced against them of the Sons of Adam, so long as they did not cast away my halter.

They were foolish in their treatment of me, and I did not control their foolishness, until I withdrew myself down to the pasterns and the hair above the hinder parts of the hoofs.

If I had been of the race of 'Ad and of Iram, brought up among them, and of Luqman and [Dhu] Jadan,

They would not have redeemed in place of their brother from a threatening danger a man of as-Sakun, and they would not have departed in respect of him from the trodden tracks.

I asked my people [to help me] — and their camels had filled full the space between Ruhbah of the thickets and al-'Adan —

What time they offered their camels to the Son of Sawwar — a splendid gift, forsooth, to be thrown away on a folly !

How did they requite [the tribe of] 'Amir with evil for their doings, or how are they requiting me with evil in return for good ?

Or how profits what a camel that smells a young one, but refuses to yield her milk to it, gives, showing affection with the nose, when there is niggardliness with the milk ?
